newsitem.title: CHINA: Shenzhen sees foreign banks in yuan business.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen sees foreign banks in yuan business.

text.p: Shenzhen Communist Party Secretary Li Youwei said on Thursday China would allow foreign banks in the southern boomtown to conduct domestic currency business, but other officials were less optimistic.
Li quoted Dai Xianglong, governor of the central People's Bank of China, as saying permission for the opening would be forthcoming.

"Dai Xianglong...clearly pointed out during a recent fact-finding visit to Shenzhen that foreign-funded banks in Shenzhen will be allowed to gradually engage in renminbi business in the not too-distant future," Li told a news conference in the city that borders Hong Kong.
He gave no timetable for when foreign banks in Shenzhen would be allowed to start transactions in the domestic yuan -- or renminbi -- currency.
China has so far given permission to nine foreign banks to conduct limited yuan currency business in China.
All have been required to set up their main branches in Shanghai's Pudong district.
Shenzhen was now host to 52 foreign-funded banks, the largest contingent in China after Shanghai, Li said.
However, Chinese officials hinted that Li's announcement may have been premature.
"We have received no formal document on this," said an official of the Shenzhen office of the central bank.

"We are carrying out research on this possibility but no decision has been reached," he said, adding that even if foreign banks were allowed to start foreign currency business the scope would be limited.
Foreign banks were enthusiastic.

"We plan to apply to do yuan business," said a senior official of the Shenzhen branch of Hong Kong's Bank of East Asia. "If we are allowed to conduct yuan business, our operations will be expanded and diversified."

"We would definitely apply to do this new business," said an official at the Shenzhen branch of Japan's Sanwa Bank. "A foreign-invested bank cannot fully develop its business unless it conducts local currency business."
In any case, their business would be restricted.

Foreign banks now operating in Shanghai are only allowed to accept deposits from foreign-funded firms or foreign individuals in Shanghai. They can only extend yuan loans to foreign-funded firms or Chinese enterprises that have previously obtained foreign currency loans from that bank.
Some of the Chinese banks that Beijing is trying to protect with its limited opening of the yuan business were also enthusiastic.
"China's market is short of capital and foreign banks can introduce more capital," a banker at one Shenzhen branch of a Chinese state-owned commercial bank said.

"The central bank must create a fair environment for foreign and Chinese banks," he said. "China must open because at the beginning you can make a favourite of your son for one, two or even 10 years. But if it lasts for 50 years then no (foreign banks) will come to China.
"So China needs a process to nurture its own banks to be competitive and introduce foreign banks gradually," he said.
He warned that Shenzhen, a Special Economic Zone created by late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, might lose out if only Shanghai were open to foreign banks for domestic currency business.
